title: BrakeClear
question: How do brakes work?
hook: Your foot pushes with 100 newtons and the pads squeeze with 7,000. Follow the push through a lever, a vacuum servo and Pascal's law, watch a disc soak up the heat of a stop, and see ABS catch a locking wheel on a wet road.

explainer.title: Brakes turn motion into heat
explainer.text: A 1,200 kg car at 100 km/h carries 463 kJ of kinetic energy. To stop, all of it must go somewhere, and brakes rub it away as heat. One pedal works four brakes through two separate circuits of fluid, split diagonally, so a burst pipe still leaves half the braking.

explainer.title: A 100 N push becomes 7 kN
explainer.text: The pedal is a 4 to 1 lever. A vacuum servo triples the push by letting air press on a diaphragm. The master cylinder turns 1,200 N into 31 bar of pressure, and by Pascal's law the same pressure reaches a caliper piston with six times the area: 7.1 kN on each pad.

explainer.title: Discs pinch, drums push out
explainer.text: A floating caliper has one piston but squeezes the disc from both sides, and its square rubber seal pulls the pads clear again. In a drum, the leading shoe is dragged into the drum and grips itself harder. That free help makes drums lose more grip than discs when their linings get hot.

explainer.title: Heat is the limit
explainer.text: One hard stop from 100 km/h warms each 5 kg front rotor by about 65 °C. Stop again and again, or ride the brakes down a long hill, and the pads pass 300 °C and fade. Hotter still, the brake fluid can boil and the pedal goes soft. A low gear lets the engine take the load instead.

explainer.title: A tyre grips best while it still turns
explainer.text: Grip peaks at about 10 to 20% slip. A locked wheel slides, grips less and cannot steer at all. ABS watches each wheel with a toothed ring and a sensor, and holds, releases and re-applies the pressure several times a second to keep the tyre near its peak.

explainer.title: Air that fails safe, motors that give back
explainer.text: Trucks and buses brake with compressed air, and a strong spring in each chamber applies the brakes if the air is lost. An electric car brakes with its motor working as a generator, putting energy back in the battery, and blends in friction brakes for the rest.

concepts.def: The energy of motion, ½ × mass × speed². Double the speed and there is four times as much to turn into heat.
The pump under the pedal that turns your push into pressure in the brake fluid. It has two pistons, one for each circuit.
Pressure put on a trapped fluid reaches every part of it equally, so a bigger piston gets a bigger force.
A diaphragm with engine vacuum on one side. Letting air in behind it adds to the driver's push, about three times over.
A disc-brake clamp with a piston on one side only. Its body slides so both pads squeeze the disc equally.
A drum-brake shoe that the turning drum drags into harder contact, so it multiplies its own grip.
Brakes working less well when very hot, because the friction of the pads or linings falls.
How much slower a braked tyre's tread moves than the road. Grip is highest at about 10 to 20% slip and lower when the wheel is locked.
Anti-lock braking system. It senses a wheel about to lock and briefly lowers that brake's pressure, so the tyre keeps gripping and steering.
